title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detectable unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the primary validator. Execution completed all planned pairs (complete_pairs = 200) and consumed 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, concrete accounting of execution volumes, the preregistered Mininet 10% holdout (20 tasks) that produced zero validator–emulator disagreements, and an artifact‑grounded discussion of methodological tradeoffs and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02).

sections.introduction: Automating natural‑language intent → device configuration translation with large language models promises operational efficiency but risks introducing incorrect or unsafe network changes. Prior work therefore proposes grounding, deterministic validation, and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to catch and correct errors before application. The practical benefit of automated repair depends on three empirical factors: (i) the baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures under the chosen generator/prompt policy; (ii) validator coverage and fidelity; and (iii) the available repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question and corresponding hypothesis: Does an automated deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? The study used a paired, shared‑initial design to isolate the marginal effect of invoking a validator (and at most one automated repair) on the identical generator output.
sections.related_work: Empirical studies and surveys across LLM applications document widespread factual errors, hallucinations, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism; mitigation approaches include retrieval grounding, verifier‑assisted repair, and constrained agent architectures [10.1007/s11704-026-60308-3; https://openalex.org/W4399803256; https://openalex.org/W4402860127]. In NetOps, prototype systems have demonstrated intent→configuration synthesis but typically lack instrumented, production‑like failure‑rate evaluations [https://openalex.org/W4399629579; https://openalex.org/W4403635865]. Architectural proposals and early prototypes recommend combining LLM generation with deterministic network validators (Batfish‑style checkers) and guarded agent patterns to reduce risk, but validator coverage and emulator fidelity remain open concerns [https://openalex.org/W4410125989; 10.36227/techrxiv.177004277.71795055/v1]. Separate red‑team and configuration‑brittleness audits show that agentic tool descriptions and multi‑tool chains can increase the attack surface and produce high‑impact safety failures if not carefully constrained [10.2139/ssrn.7203631; 10.21203/rs.3.rs-10646209/v1]. Our study contributes an externally auditable, preregistered measurement that isolates the incremental effect of deterministic validation+repair for a fixed model and sampling policy.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The study preregistration (study_id = cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) fixed a paired design with n = 200 tasks, a shared deterministic initial generation per task (one API call shared across both conditions), and a repair budget of at most one automated repair call per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the confirmatory test was an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs were computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) as preregistered for inferential completeness. Power planning assumed a baseline unsafe incidence ≈30% and a target 50% relative reduction; these assumptions justified the n = 200 sample but do not influence the observed outcomes.

Task bank, validators, and holdout. We used a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration task bank of 200 tasks stratified across four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task encodes initial and expected final states plus workflow constraints (e.g., make_before_break, must_be_down_for_fields) and a required_sequence that the deterministic validator checks. The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforces syntax and intent/constraint checks and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as an independent disagreement detector and applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to surface validator blind spots.

Shared‑initial adapter semantics and determinism reconciliation. The execution adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task the system produced one initial candidate that was reused for both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. The preregistration described a deterministic generation policy (temperature = 0) for the shared initial candidate. In the archived execution artifacts the runtime model configuration file records temperature = null; this is a metadata difference between preregistration text and the recorded configuration artifact. Crucially, deterministic execution accounting artifacts (deterministic_reconciliation and the provider call audit summarized in the execution manifest) empirically confirm single shared initial invocations per task (hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; stage_counts indicate shared_initial_generation = 200). Thus, regardless of the temperature metadata field value, the adapter semantics and execution accounting produce an empirical single‑draw, shared‑initial design that enforces the intended paired causal contrast. We report this factual reconciliation and cite the archived execution bundle for audit (see archived execution manifest and deterministic reconciliation artifacts listed in the artifact bundle).

Repair policy, budgeting, and contamination handling. When the primary validator reported violations, the preregistered policy allowed at most one automated repair prompt to the same LLM; any repaired candidate would be revalidated by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and recorded. The execution contract enforced a maximum model‑call cap of 400 (200 initial + up to 200 repairs); the adapter enforced that cap. The contamination plan deterministically excluded from the primary analysis any pairs flagged by the Mininet emulator (Batfish‑style validator verdict != Mininet verdict). The 10% Mininet holdout executed as preregistered to check validator–emulator agreement.

Reproducibility notes and a documented gap. All seeds and model‑call logs were archived. We disclose a reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized selection seed used to draw the Mininet 10% holdout is not present as a labeled artifact in the archive, which prevents exact bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of the holdout draw even though the contamination summary reports zero disagreements for the holdout. We make this limitation explicit here and in the Disclosure Statement.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run executed to completion under the frozen preregistered plan (start and end timestamps archived in the execution manifest). Accounting: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across conditions), complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task), maximum_model_calls = 400, repair_calls_used = 0. Deterministic reconciliation artifacts confirm hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, evidencing the shared single invocation per task.

Primary outcomes. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. The prespecified exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile confidence intervals (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) produce a 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Under the preregistered estimand and test the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis is not evaluable because baseline validator failures are absent.

Repair and secondary outcomes. Because no validator failures were observed, the preregistered repair branch was never invoked and the secondary estimands (average repair iterations per repaired task, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair) have no empirical data from this run.

Mininet holdout contamination check. The preregistered Mininet 10% holdout (20 tasks) produced zero validator–emulator disagreements per the contamination_summary artifact, so the conservative exclusion branch was not activated. We reiterate that the exact randomized holdout selection seed is not labeled in the archive, which limits deterministic reconstruction of which specific tasks comprised the holdout despite the zero‑disagreement result.

Representative diagnostics. Archived per‑task validator traces for representative pairs show validation_before and validation_after valid = true, violation_count = 0, and parsed_command_count matching required_command_count for tasks labeled with difficulty levels ("medium", "hard", "very_hard") and patterns such as make_before_break_uplink_switchover and paired_link_atomic_mtu_change—evidence that the task bank exercised nontrivial workflow constraints even when outputs were validator‑satisfying.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The confirmatory outcome is a precise, artifact‑grounded null: both baseline and GVR conditions produced validator‑passing configurations for every task in the sampled bank, yielding no discordant pairs. This is not evidence that repair is never useful; rather it is a statement that, under the frozen design (single shared initial draw, one possible automated repair, the chosen generator/prompt policy, and the particular task bank), there were no validator‑detectable failures for GVR to reduce. Practically, the marginal utility of automated repair depends on baseline failure prevalence and validator coverage for the workload of interest.

Methodological tradeoffs. The shared‑initial paired design isolates the causal marginal effect of validation+repair on a fixed generator output but intentionally excludes gains achievable via multi‑sample generation (re‑sampling) or nonzero‑temperature sampling that may surface diverse failing candidates. Evaluators interested in unconditional failure rates and unconditional repair gains should therefore adopt designs with per‑condition independent sampling and multiple draws per task. Our archived artifacts and execution accounting provide a reproducible template for either design family, subject to the noted holdout‑seed gap.

Validator coverage and emulator corroboration. Deterministic validators codify a set of syntactic and workflow checks but cannot represent all device idiosyncrasies. The Mininet holdout was included as a pragmatic independent check; the zero disagreements observed in the 20‑task holdout suggests no obvious validator blind spots were detected in that sample, but holdout scale and the missing labeled seed limit the strength of that corroboration. Robust operational assurance requires richer validators, larger emulation sampling, and adversarial probing to reveal latent blind spots.

Operational implications. If baseline validator failures are rare for a production generator/prompt policy, a narrow repair budget (one automated repair) yields limited marginal benefit for validator‑detectable errors; investments may instead target increasing validator fidelity, adversarial testing, or multi‑sample generation strategies. Conversely, if baseline failure prevalence is nontrivial, GVR with larger repair budgets and multi‑step repair strategies can reduce validator‑detected errors—design choices that future confirmatory studies should preregister and measure.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), resulting in an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Because baseline validator failures were absent, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated on this sample. The artifact‑grounded outcome emphasizes that GVR’s measured marginal value is workload dependent: when validator‑detectable failures are rare under the tested generation policy, automated repair provides no measured reduction in those validator‑detected errors. Future work should preregister designs that target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, expand validator fidelity (larger emulation or real‑device checks), evaluate multi‑sample and multi‑model policies, and explore multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets to characterize practical operational gains. All execution and analysis artifacts referenced in this manuscript are archived under the preregistration id cited above for independent inspection.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: orchestration used hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the deterministic task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Primary deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). A Mininet‑based emulator was preregistered and executed as a secondary disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks); the archived contamination summary reports zero disagreements for that holdout but the explicit randomized selection seed for the holdout is not present as a labeled artifact in the archive (documented reproducibility gap). Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls. Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan (start and end times recorded in the execution manifest); model calls, prompts, seeds, validator traces, emulator traces, logs, and the artifact manifest are archived in the execution bundle. Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Known reproducibility gap: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact deterministic reconstruction of the drawn holdout despite the contamination summary reporting no disagreements. The archived execution manifest and deterministic reconciliation artifacts provide execution accounting (hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; stage_counts indicate shared_initial_generation = 200) that empirically confirm the single shared initial invocation per task.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested. Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
